title: Simplifying Implant-Supported Overdenture Prosthetics: A Digital Workflow
html:
Written by: Drs. Joc Jernigan and Gregori M. Kurtzman

INTRODUCTION

Implant-supported overdentures have become a predictable treatment option for rehabilitating edentulous patients, providing significantly greater retention, stability, masticatory efficiency, patient satisfaction, and oral health-related quality of life than conventional complete dentures.1-4 Advances in implant design, digital treatment planning, intraoral scanning, and CAD/CAM manufacturing have further improved restorative precision and treatment efficiency.5-7 Despite these advances, accurately transferring implant position while preserving the patient’s established occlusion, vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO), tooth arrangement, facial support, phonetics, and soft tissue contours remains a challenge in full-arch implant prosthodontics. Conventional implant impressions remain accurate but are technique-sensitive and require multiple clinical and laboratory procedures.8-10

The ArchBridge for Overdenture digital workflow (ROE Dental Laboratory) addresses these limitations by combining uniquely identifiable scan bodies with digital capture of the patient’s existing denture or overdenture (Figure 1a). Rather than serving solely as a digital impression technique, the workflow creates a comprehensive virtual record incorporating implant position, soft tissue anatomy, occlusion, VDO, and established prosthetic contours. Using the patient’s existing prosthesis as a restorative template preserves clinically validated records while enabling a completely digital, model-free laboratory workflow utilizing a proprietary patent-pending processing technique for the overdenture housings.

Perhaps the greatest advantage of this approach is the completely digital workflow extending from the clinician’s office to the laboratory. Analog impressions, stone models, and chairside pickup of the attachment housings are eliminated, reducing treatment time while improving communication between the practice and laboratory. A permanent digital archive provides an additional long-term benefit by allowing future repairs, duplicate prostheses, replacement overdentures, or conversion to a fixed implant restoration to be completed with substantially fewer clinical procedures.

This article describes the clinical application of the ArchBridge for Overdenture digital workflow, outlines the clinical and laboratory procedures, and discusses how complete digital preservation of implant and prosthetic information can simplify fabrication while improving long-term maintenance of implant-supported overdentures.

Clinical Significance

The ArchBridge for Overdenture workflow combines uniquely identifiable scan bodies with digital capture of the patient’s existing denture or overdenture to create a comprehensive digital record of implant position, soft tissue contours, occlusion, VDO, and established tooth arrangement. Rather than recreating clinically validated records, the existing prosthesis serves as the restorative template, allowing aesthetics, phonetics, facial support, and occlusal relationships to transfer directly to the definitive prosthesis.

The greatest advantage of this workflow is the completely digital process from the clinician’s office through the laboratory. Conventional impressions, stone models, and chairside pickup of the retentive housings are eliminated, while a proprietary patent-pending laboratory technique allows the housings to be processed directly from digital records in a completely model-free workflow. This reduces chair time, simplifies laboratory procedures, and streamlines communication between the practice and laboratory.

An additional benefit is the creation of a permanent digital archive. Because implant and prosthetic information are preserved electronically, future repairs, relines, duplicate prostheses, replacement overdentures, or conversion to a fixed implant restoration can often be completed with substantially fewer clinical procedures, improving long-term maintenance and restorative efficiency.

Technique for Digital Implant Overdenture Prosthetics

Digital workflows continue to improve implant prosthodontics by simplifying communication between the clinician and laboratory while reducing the clinical and laboratory procedures required to fabricate implant-supported restorations. Although intraoral scanning has become routine for many restorative procedures, accurately capturing multiple implants across a completely edentulous arch remains challenging because of the limited anatomic landmarks available for image stitching.11-15

The ArchBridge for Overdenture workflow addresses these limitations by combining uniquely identifiable scan bodies with digital capture of the patient’s existing prosthesis and a proprietary patent-pending processing technique that enables a completely model-free laboratory workflow. Unlike conventional scan bodies that rely primarily on surface geometry, the ArchBridge scan bodies create a distinctive 3D reference pattern that improves digital registration of implant position, angulation, and rotational orientation while reducing the potential for stitching errors.

The greatest advantage of this workflow is that it remains completely digital from the clinician’s office through the laboratory. Conventional analog impressions, poured models, and chairside pickup of the LOCATOR housings are eliminated. Instead, the laboratory utilizes a proprietary patent-pending digital process to accurately incorporate the retentive housings directly from the digital records without analog transfer procedures. This simplifies treatment, reduces chair time, minimizes technique-sensitive steps, and improves communication between the practice and laboratory.

Following placement of the LOCATOR abutments (Zest Dental Solutions), the ArchBridge scan bodies are attached intraorally and an intraoral scan records implant position, angulation, rotational orientation, and the surrounding soft tissues. The existing overdenture is relieved as necessary to ensure passive seating, relined with light-body polyvinyl siloxane (PVS), and scanned extraorally to capture both the polished and intaglio surfaces. Digital scans of the opposing arch and the interocclusal relationship complete the virtual patient record.

The laboratory merges these datasets into a single digital model reproducing implant position, soft tissue anatomy, occlusion, VDO, and prosthetic contours. The definitive overdenture is then designed using CAD/CAM technology while preserving the patient’s established aesthetics, occlusion, and tooth arrangement. Because these clinical records have already been validated, additional jaw relation records and aesthetic try-in appointments may often be reduced or eliminated.

A permanent digital archive represents an important long-term benefit. Implant positions, prosthetic design, and restorative records can be stored indefinitely and retrieved for repairs, duplicate prostheses, replacement overdentures, or future conversion to a fixed implant restoration. By preserving both implant and prosthetic information, the ArchBridge for Overdenture workflow provides an efficient and predictable digital solution for implant-supported overdenture therapy.

Clinical Technique

Treatment begins following successful osseointegration or, in immediate-load cases, after placement of the definitive overdenture abutments. Before initiating the digital workflow, the existing prosthesis is evaluated to verify aesthetics, VDO, centric occlusion, phonetics, and lip support. Because these parameters have already been clinically validated, they serve as the foundation for the definitive prosthesis.

After removal of the prosthesis, the healing abutments are replaced with the definitive LOCATOR overdenture abutments according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. ArchBridge scan bodies are attached to each abutment (Figure 1b). Their unique geometry provides stable seating and accurate digital registration of implant position, angulation, and rotational orientation during intraoral scanning.

Following completion of the implant scan, the scan bodies are removed, and the existing denture is relieved as necessary to ensure passive seating over the LOCATOR abutments. Light-body PVS is placed within the intaglio surface, and the prosthesis is seated until polymerization to accurately record the functional soft tissue contours while preserving the established occlusal relationship.

The relined denture is then scanned extraorally to capture both the polished and intaglio surfaces. Digital scans of the opposing arch and an interocclusal record complete the virtual patient record. These files are transmitted electronically to the laboratory, where the implant scan, overdenture scan, opposing arch, and bite registration are merged into a single digital model (Figure 1c). This comprehensive dataset preserves implant position, tooth arrangement, VDO, occlusion, and aesthetics for CAD/CAM design of the definitive overdenture. When a milled implant bar is prescribed, a CAD/CAM verification jig may be fabricated to confirm passive intraoral fit before fabrication of the definitive framework.16,17

At delivery, the definitive overdenture is evaluated for complete seating, retention, stability, occlusion, aesthetics, phonetics, and oral hygiene access. Minor occlusal adjustments are completed as necessary before the patient is instructed in prosthesis insertion, removal, hygiene, and long-term maintenance.

Case Example

A patient wearing an implant-retained mandibular overdenture presented with a fractured prosthesis requiring replacement. Clinical examination confirmed stable osseointegrated implants, healthy peri-implant tissues, and satisfactory implant distribution. Because the existing overdenture provided acceptable aesthetics, occlusion, phonetics, and VDO, it was selected as the restorative template for fabrication of the new prosthesis.

Following removal of the overdenture, definitive LOCATOR abutments were placed and ArchBridge scan bodies attached (Figures 2 to 5). An intraoral scan captured implant position, angulation, rotational orientation, and the surrounding soft tissues. The existing overdenture was relieved, relined with light-body PVS, and scanned extraorally to record both the polished and intaglio surfaces (Figures 6 to 8). Digital scans of the opposing arch and the interocclusal relationship completed the virtual patient record.

The digital files were transmitted electronically to the laboratory, where they were merged into a single dataset preserving implant position, tooth arrangement, occlusion, VDO, and prosthetic contours. A CAD/CAM verification jig was fabricated to confirm passive intraoral fit before processing the definitive overdenture (Figures 9 to 11). Using a proprietary patent-pending model-free digital workflow, the LOCATOR housings were incorporated directly from the digital records without conventional analog procedures.

The definitive overdenture demonstrated excellent fit, retention, stability, aesthetics, phonetics, and occlusion (Figures 12 to 16). Because the patient’s established prosthetic relationships were preserved throughout the digital workflow, only minimal occlusal adjustment was required at delivery.

DISCUSSION

Implant-supported overdentures remain one of the most predictable and cost-effective treatment options for edentulous patients, consistently improving retention, stability, masticatory function, comfort, and patient satisfaction compared with conventional complete dentures.1-4 As digital technologies continue to evolve, clinicians increasingly seek workflows that improve accuracy while reducing treatment complexity and clinical appointments.

The ArchBridge for Overdenture workflow differs from conventional digital impression techniques by capturing not only implant position but also the patient’s existing prosthesis as a validated restorative template. By digitally preserving tooth arrangement, VDO, centric occlusion, facial support, phonetics, and soft tissue contours, the workflow minimizes the need to recreate clinical records that have already been successfully established.

As mentioned earlier, the greatest advantage of this system is the completely digital workflow extending from the clinician’s office through the laboratory. Conventional implant impressions, stone casts, analog transfers, and chairside pickup of the LOCATOR housings are eliminated. Instead, a proprietary patent-pending model-free laboratory process accurately incorporates the retentive housings directly from the digital records, reducing technique-sensitive laboratory procedures while improving communication between the clinician and laboratory.

Digital preservation of the patient’s established prosthetic relationships also contributes to clinical efficiency. Because aesthetics, occlusion, VDO, and tooth arrangement are transferred directly from the existing prosthesis, fewer clinical records are required, and delivery of the definitive overdenture often requires only minor occlusal refinement. This streamlined workflow can reduce chair time while maintaining restorative accuracy.

Another important advantage is the creation of a permanent digital archive. Implant positions, prosthetic design files, and occlusal records remain available indefinitely, allowing duplicate prostheses, repairs, relines, replacement overdentures, or conversion to a fixed implant restoration to be completed with substantially fewer clinical procedures. This provides long-term value for both clinicians and patients while simplifying future maintenance.

Although the workflow requires familiarity with digital scanning protocols and coordination with a laboratory utilizing the proprietary ArchBridge process, these considerations are offset by reduced analog procedures, improved efficiency, and enhanced reproducibility. As digital implant prosthodontics continues to advance, workflows that integrate comprehensive digital records with model-free laboratory fabrication are likely to play an increasingly important role in implant-supported overdenture therapy.

CONCLUSION

The ArchBridge for Overdenture workflow represents an important advancement in the digital fabrication of implant-supported overdentures by creating a completely digital workflow from the clinician’s office through the laboratory. Using uniquely identifiable scan bodies and a proprietary, patent-pending, model-free laboratory processing technique, the system accurately transfers implant position, soft tissue anatomy, occlusion, VDO, and established prosthetic contours without conventional impressions, stone models, or chairside pickup of the retentive housings.

By preserving the patient’s existing prosthesis as the restorative template, clinicians can reproduce clinically validated aesthetics, phonetics, occlusion, and tooth arrangement while reducing treatment complexity and improving communication between the clinician and laboratory. In addition, the permanent digital archive simplifies future repairs, duplicate prostheses, replacement overdentures, and potential conversion to fixed implant restorations with substantially fewer clinical procedures.

As digital implant dentistry continues to evolve, workflows that eliminate analog procedures while improving efficiency, reproducibility, and long-term restorative maintenance will play an increasingly important role in implant prosthodontics. The ArchBridge for Overdenture system provides clinicians with a practical and predictable approach that streamlines treatment while preserving the restorative information needed for efficient long-term patient care.

This article was adapted from “The ArchBridge Digitally Integrated Workflow: A Fully Digital, Model-Free Workflow for Implant-Supported Overdenture Rehabilitation,” by Joc Jernigan and Gregori M. Kurtzman, published online 2026 Aug 27 in Cureus.
